title: The coronation of Mary I
shortBlurb: Crowned at Westminster by the Bishop of Winchester, Mary Tudor became the first queen of England anointed in her own right…
body: When Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, the Duke of Northumberland's devise set aside the king's half-sisters for Lady Jane Grey, proclaimed on 10 July. The country would not have her; within nine days Mary's cause had prevailed, and on 3 August she entered London in triumph.

On Sunday 1 October 1553 she was crowned in Westminster Abbey by Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — the Archbishop of Canterbury being a prisoner in the Tower. It was done, the old account notes, in spite of the excommunication that still lay upon the country; the conduits at Cornhill and Cheapside ran with wine.

She was the first woman anointed queen of England in her own right. Within two years Parliament had restored the old worship and received Cardinal Pole as legate, reconciling the realm to the Apostolic See. The restoration lasted barely five years, and is remembered more for the fires of Smithfield than for the coronation pomp.

title: The fall of Jerusalem to Saladin
shortBlurb: Eighty-eight years after the crusaders took it, Jerusalem opened its gates to Saladin, and the Latin kingdom was left a coastal remnant…
body: On 4 July 1187, at the horns of Hattin above Tiberias, Saladin destroyed the army of the Latin kingdom, taking King Guy and the relic of the True Cross. City after city then surrendered — Acre, Jaffa, Beirut, Ascalon — until Jerusalem itself, crowded with refugees, stood alone under Balian of Ibelin.

After a short siege Balian obtained terms, and on 2 October 1187, the anniversary, it was noted, of the Prophet's night journey, the city opened its gates. The Latin dominion over Jerusalem had lasted eighty-eight years. Unlike the conquerors of 1099, Saladin forbade a general massacre: the inhabitants were ransomed at ten dinars a man, though thousands who could not pay were led into captivity.

The shock summoned the Third Crusade; Richard of England and Philip of France recovered a strip of coast but never the city. Save for a brief treaty interlude in the thirteenth century, Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands for more than seven centuries.

title: Paul VI before the United Nations
shortBlurb: On the feast of St. Francis, Paul VI crossed the Atlantic for a one-day visit to plead before the nations: no more war, war never again…
body: On 4 October 1965, the feast of St. Francis of Assisi, Paul VI landed in New York — the first pope to set foot in the Western Hemisphere, and the first to leave Italy since 1809. "Greetings to you, America," he said at the airport; "the first pope to set foot on your land blesses you with all his heart."

Greeted by Secretary-General U Thant, he addressed the General Assembly in French, in the organization's twentieth year. "No more war, war never again," he pleaded; "it is peace, peace, that has to guide the destiny of the nations of all mankind." The whole journey lasted fourteen hours and ended with Mass at Yankee Stadium.

In Rome the Second Vatican Council was then holding its fourth and last session; two months later, on 8 December 1965, the pope closed it. His one-day pilgrimage for peace set a pattern: his successors have returned to the same rostrum to speak for the Church before the family of nations.

sources.text: Paul VI, Address to the United Nations Organization, 4 October 1965 (vatican.va)

title: The Fourth Council of Constantinople opens
shortBlurb: Legates of Pope Hadrian II opened in Hagia Sophia the council the West would number as the eighth general synod, called to end the affair of Photius…
body: The patriarch Ignatius, deposed and exiled years before, had been restored by the new emperor Basil the Macedonian; the intruded Photius, who had gone so far as to pronounce the deposition of Pope Nicholas I in 867, was confined to a monastery. Both emperor and patriarch asked Rome for a general council, and Hadrian II sent three legates to preside in his name.

On 5 October 869 the council opened in the cathedral of Holy Wisdom, the pope's legates in the first seats. The fathers were never many — little more than a hundred bishops in all — and over ten sessions, the last on 28 February 870, they reconciled the penitent, heard a silent and unyielding Photius, renewed his condemnation, and subscribed the old formula of Hormisdas binding its signers to the Apostolic See.

Western canonists number this as the eighth ecumenical council, though the East has not received it into her synodal books. Within a decade Ignatius was dead and Photius reigned again in his place, and a further council in 879 undid much of what the council of 869 had decreed.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Constantinople, Fourth Ecumenical Council of”

title: The death of William Tyndale
shortBlurb: Strangled and burned at Vilvoorde for giving England the Scriptures in her own tongue, Tyndale left a translation that underlies the English Bible to this day…
body: Tyndale, a priest formed at Oxford and Cambridge, held that the plowboy should know the Scripture as well as the prelate. Driven abroad, he translated the New Testament from the Greek and began printing it at Cologne in 1525; stopped there, he finished the work at Worms, and in the summer of 1526 three thousand copies were smuggled into England.

For a decade he lived in hiding on the Continent, adding the Pentateuch and Jonah to his work, while the bishops burned his books and the king's agents hunted him. Betrayed at Antwerp by a false friend, he was held in the castle of Vilvoorde near Brussels and condemned for heresy.

On 6 October 1536, by the reckoning of his earliest biographers, he was strangled at the stake and his body burned, crying — so the martyrologist Foxe records — "Lord, open the King of England's eyes." Within three years an English Bible stood in every parish church; and his renderings, revised but never replaced, still form the bone and sinew of the English versions.

title: The Council of Chalcedon opens
shortBlurb: The largest assembly of bishops the ancient Church had yet seen gathered in the church of St. Euphemia to confess one Christ in two natures…
body: The emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria had summoned the bishops to Nicaea, then brought them nearer the capital, to Chalcedon on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus. There, on 8 October 451, in the church of the martyr St. Euphemia, the fourth general council opened — some five or six hundred bishops, nearly all from the East, the greatest number any council had yet gathered.

The legates of St. Leo the Great presided, imperial commissioners ordering the outer business. The acts of the Robber Synod of Ephesus were read; Dioscorus of Alexandria, its author, was removed from his seat and later deposed; and Leo's letter to Flavian, the Tome, was acclaimed with the cry that Peter had spoken through Leo.

In its Definition the council confessed one and the same Christ, Son and Lord, in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The sessions ran to 1 November; Marcian himself attended the sixth, on 25 October. One canon, the twenty-eighth, exalting the see of Constantinople, Rome would never accept.

title: The death of Pope Pius XII
shortBlurb: Eugenio Pacelli, who had guided the Church through world war and defined the Assumption, died at Castel Gandolfo after nineteen years as pope…
body: Eugenio Pacelli was born in Rome on 2 March 1876, and on his sixty-third birthday, 2 March 1939, was elected pope, taking the name Pius XII. Within months Europe was at war, and his pontificate was bound up with the war years: his first encyclical, Summi Pontificatus, and his radio appeal of August 1939 warned of the gathering storm.

His nineteen years saw the definition of the Assumption of Our Lady, proclaimed on 1 November 1950 in the bull Munificentissimus Deus, and a great quickening of the Church's liturgical and scholarly life; his wartime silences and charities alike have been debated ever since.

Stricken by a stroke at his summer residence, he died at Castel Gandolfo in the small hours of 9 October 1958, and was buried in the grottoes of St. Peter's. Nineteen days later the conclave chose the Patriarch of Venice, who took the name John XXIII — and within months astonished the world by summoning a council.

title: The Battle of Tours
shortBlurb: Charles, Mayor of the Palace, broke the advance of the armies of al-Andalus between Tours and Poitiers, and won the name of the Hammer…
body: Twenty years after the conquest of Spain, Abd al-Rahman, governor of al-Andalus, crossed the Pyrenees with a great host, defeated Duke Eudes of Aquitaine, and drove north toward the Loire, pillaging as he went. Eudes turned for help to his old rival Charles, Mayor of the Palace in Austrasia.

In October 732 — the day is variously reckoned the 10th or the 25th of the month — the two armies met on the road between Tours and Poitiers. The Frankish foot stood like a wall, the chroniclers say; Abd al-Rahman was slain, and by nightfall his army was in flight, leaving its plunder and its tents.

The old Catholic judgment calls it one of the great events in the history of the world; later ages named the victor Martellus, the Hammer. Whether one battle or a season of campaigning turned the tide, the armies of the caliphate never again struck so deep into Gaul, and Charles's grandson would be crowned at Rome as Charlemagne.

title: The Battle of Hastings
shortBlurb: On Senlac Hill near Hastings, King Harold fell with his brothers, and William of Normandy's victory began the remaking of England and her Church…
body: Harold had been king nine months. On 25 September 1066 he destroyed the invading Norsemen at Stamford Bridge; three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey, carrying — the Norman writers say — a banner blessed by Pope Alexander II. Forced marches brought Harold south to meet him with a weary army.

The battle was fought on 14 October 1066 on the hill of Senlac, seven miles from Hastings, and lasted from morning to dusk. The old account remarks the temper of the two camps the night before: the Normans prayed and prepared for Communion while the English caroused. By nightfall Harold and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine lay dead, and with them the flower of the English thegnhood.

William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day. The Conquest remade the English Church as well as the realm: Stigand was deposed and Lanfranc of Bec came to Canterbury, councils reformed the clergy, and new cathedrals rose in the Norman manner. On the battlefield itself William raised Battle Abbey, its high altar over the spot where Harold fell.

title: The Nobel Peace Prize for Mother Teresa
shortBlurb: The Norwegian committee's choice fell on the nun of Calcutta, who received the world's most famous prize in the name of the poorest of the poor…
body: On 17 October 1979 the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that the Peace Prize would go to Mother Teresa of Calcutta, "for work undertaken in the struggle to overcome poverty and distress, which also constitutes a threat to peace."

She was born Gonxha Agnes Bojaxhiu at Skopje in 1910, had gone to India as a Loreto sister, and in 1946, on the train to Darjeeling, received what she called her "call within a call." The congregation she founded, the Missionaries of Charity, established at Calcutta on 7 October 1950, served the dying and the destitute of the city's streets.

At Oslo on 10 December she asked that the money for the customary banquet be given to the poor, and received the prize, as her own words had it, "for the glory of God and in the name of the poor." She died in 1997; John Paul II beatified her in 2003, and she was enrolled among the saints in 2016.

title: The revocation of the Edict of Nantes
shortBlurb: By the Edict of Fontainebleau Louis XIV revoked the toleration of 1598, silenced the Reformed churches, and scattered the Huguenots across the world…
body: For fourscore and seven years the Edict of Nantes, granted by Henry IV in 1598, had given the Reformed of France a measured toleration. Under Louis XIV the measure was steadily withdrawn, church by church and office by office, until on 18 October 1685 the king signed at Fontainebleau the edict that revoked his grandfather's grant altogether.

Public worship was forbidden to the Protestants, their churches razed, their ministers ordered from the realm within fifteen days; parents were commanded to have their children baptized and schooled as Catholics; and emigration was banned for men on pain of the galleys, for women of prison.

The blow was applauded in France — Vauban and Saint-Simon were nearly alone in deploring it — yet it scattered a multitude: Vauban reckoned a hundred thousand Frenchmen lost to the kingdom, with sixty million livres, nine thousand sailors, and the best of her officers gone to her enemies. The proscribed worship lived on in secret assemblies "in the desert," and flared into the Camisard war of the Cévennes in 1702.

title: The marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella
shortBlurb: In a private house at Valladolid the heirs of Aragon and Castile were wed in secret, joining the crowns from which a united Spain would rise…
body: Isabella was eighteen, the chosen heiress of Castile; Ferdinand seventeen, heir of Aragon. Their marriage had been long negotiated against the will of her brother King Henry, and was therefore done in secret: the princess slipped away from the court, and Ferdinand crossed Castile disguised as a muleteer with a handful of companions.

On the morning of 19 October 1469, in the house of Juan de Vivero at Valladolid, the Archbishop of Toledo married them. They stood within the forbidden degrees of kinship, and the dispensation shown that day — a bull in the name of a pope already dead — was of doubtful warrant until a true one came from Rome. There was no pomp: money had to be borrowed for the wedding feast.

From that union the two crowns moved as one. Isabella succeeded to Castile in 1474, Ferdinand to Aragon in 1479; together they took Granada in 1492, sent Columbus across the Ocean Sea in the same year, and were styled by the pope the Catholic Monarchs. Their grandson would reign as the Emperor Charles V.

title: The Crusaders before Antioch
shortBlurb: Two years after Clermont, the host of the First Crusade crossed the Taurus and sat down before the walls of Antioch for its most terrible siege…
body: The armies that answered Urban II at Clermont fared better than the poor pilgrims who went before them. In June 1097 they took Nicaea; on the first of July they routed the Turks at Dorylaeum; then, through a burning summer, they crossed the length of Asia Minor.

On 20 October 1097 they came before Antioch, the ancient city of the disciples, girdled — the old account numbers them — by a wall with four hundred and fifty towers, and provisioned for a long defense by its governor Yaghi-Siyan. Too strong to storm and too large to surround, the city held the crusaders before it for more than seven months of hunger, desertion, and winter rain.

Antioch fell at last on the night of 2-3 June 1098, betrayed by the captain of a single tower; and within days the besiegers were themselves besieged by the relieving army of Kerbogha of Mosul, whom they defeated on 28 June. The way to Jerusalem lay open, though the host did not take it until the next year.

title: The destruction of the People's Crusade
shortBlurb: The unarmed thousands who had set out for Jerusalem under Peter the Hermit marched into a Turkish ambush, and the People's Crusade ended in a day…
body: Before the princes had gathered their armies, the preaching of the crusade moved the poor. Tens of thousands followed Peter the Hermit and the knight Walter the Pennyless across Europe to Constantinople in the summer of 1096, plundering as they came; the emperor Alexius, to be rid of them, ferried them across the Bosphorus into Turkish territory.

There the host fell to quarreling along national lines. A German band that had seized the castle of Xerigordos was starved into surrender and destroyed; and when rumor came that the same men had taken Nicaea itself, the main body would wait no longer for Peter, who had gone back to Constantinople for supplies.

On the morning of 21 October 1096 the whole multitude, leaving women and children in the camp, marched out toward Nicaea and into the ambush of Kilij Arslan's Turks near Civetot. It was less a battle than a slaughter; Walter fell, pierced by seven arrows, and only a few thousand, rescued by Byzantine ships, returned to tell the tale. The princes' crusade, when it came, marched under discipline — and fared otherwise.

title: The death of Charles Martel
shortBlurb: The Hammer of Tours died at Quierzy, having shielded Boniface's mission and raised the Frankish power his grandson Charlemagne would crown…
body: Charles was the natural son of Pepin of Herstal, and had fought his way from prison to the mastery of the Frankish realm, ruling as Mayor of the Palace while the later Merovingian kings reigned in name. For a quarter century he campaigned without rest — against Frisians, Saxons, Bavarians, Alemanni, and the Moslem hosts of Spain.

His name in history rests on the October day of 732 when he broke the army of Abd al-Rahman between Tours and Poitiers. But the Church knew him also as the shield of her missionaries: St. Boniface worked under his protection from 723, and wrote that without it he could neither govern his flock nor defend his clergy; under Charles the Bavarian Church was ordered into the dioceses of Salzburg, Regensburg, Freising, and Passau.

He died at Quierzy on the Oise on 22 October 741 — some of the older authorities say the 21st — and was buried with the kings at Saint-Denis, though later ages, for his seizure of Church lands, made him the subject of a fearful legend of damnation. His realm he divided between his sons Carloman and Pepin; his grandson was Charlemagne.

title: The Irish rising of 1641
shortBlurb: On an October night the Ulster Irish rose for faith and land, beginning eleven years of war that ended at Drogheda and Wexford…
body: The grievances were old: the plantation of Ulster had settled Scottish and English colonists on confiscated lands, the penal laws pressed upon the Catholic gentry, and rumor ran that the Puritan Parliament meant worse. In the autumn of 1641 the dispossessed lords of the north conspired to seize the strong places of Ireland in one night.

The stroke fell on the night of 22-23 October 1641. Sir Phelim O'Neill took the fort of Charlemont by surprise and proclaimed that he rose for the king and the defense of religion and liberty; but the sister plot against Dublin Castle was betrayed on the very eve, and the capital held. Within a week the rising had spread through eight counties of Ulster.

What followed defies easy telling: thousands of settlers were killed or driven out — the numbers were wildly swollen in the English pamphlets, and are contested still — and the Catholic gentry of the Pale joined the northern men to form the Confederation of Kilkenny in 1642. The wars ran eleven years, until Cromwell landed at Dublin in 1649.

title: The consecration of Chartres Cathedral
shortBlurb: Rebuilt in a generation after the great fire, Notre-Dame de Chartres was consecrated in the presence of St. Louis, her windows already the wonder of Christendom…
body: When fire gutted the Romanesque cathedral of Chartres in 1194, the town's despair turned to hope when the relic of the Virgin's veil — brought from Aachen by Charles the Bald about 876 — was found unharmed. Kings, guilds, and peasants gave or dragged stone, and in little more than a generation the new church rose, the most perfectly Gothic of all cathedrals.

The consecration came in October 1260 — the 24th by the common reckoning, though some authorities give the 17th — and St. Louis is believed to have attended with his mother Blanche of Castile. The royal house had given richly: the upper windows were the gift of the king, of St. Ferdinand, and of the queen mother.

Her glass is her glory: the old count numbers near four thousand figures in her windows. Kings came to her as pilgrims — Henry III of France eighteen times, Charles V of France twice, and barefoot; and Henry IV, barred from Reims, was crowned at Chartres in 1594. The Revolution spared her, and two wars; she stands as she was consecrated.

title: The abdication of Charles V
shortBlurb: In the great hall at Brussels the emperor on whom the sun never set laid down his crowns, leaning on the shoulder of William the Silent…
body: He had ruled an empire of which it was said that the sun never set: Spain and the Indies, the Low Countries, Naples and Milan, Austria and the Empire itself. Worn by gout and by forty years of war against France, the Turk, and the Reformation, Charles V resolved to end his days in a cloister.

On 25 October 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg palace at Brussels where forty years before he had been declared of age, he resigned the Netherlands to his son Philip before the States General. Leaning on the shoulder of the young William of Orange — later called the Silent — the emperor numbered his journeys: ten to the Low Countries, nine to Germany, seven to Spain, seven to Italy, four to France, two to England, two to Africa. "My life has been one long journey."

In January 1556 he resigned Spain and the Indies; in August, the imperial crown to his brother Ferdinand, though the electors did not accept the resignation until 1558. He withdrew to the monastery of Yuste in Estremadura, and died there on 21 September 1558, holding the cross his wife Isabella had held in death.

title: The death of Alfred the Great
shortBlurb: The king who saved Christian Wessex from the Danes, and taught his people to read again, died at Winchester, the only English king called the Great…
body: Alfred was born at Wantage in 849, the fifth son of King Ethelwulf, and came to the throne of Wessex in 871 with the Danish host at the gates. In 878, driven to the marshes of Athelney, he rallied, broke the Danes at Ethandun, and stood godfather at the font to their king Guthrum.

The peace he won he used for the Church's repair. Lamenting that learning had perished from England, he gathered scholars and himself translated into the English tongue Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule and Dialogues, Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Orosius's history of the world, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History; his reign saw the beginnings of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and a code of laws prefaced with the law of God.

He died on 26 October 899, not yet fifty-one, and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. Posterity has named him alone of English kings "the Great"; the old writers called him England's darling and the shepherd of his people.

title: The Assisi Day of Prayer for Peace
shortBlurb: At John Paul II's invitation the leaders of the world's religions kept a day of fasting and prayer for peace in the city of St. Francis…
body: In the autumn of 1986, with the cold war still upon the world, John Paul II invited the leaders of the Christian Churches and of the other great religions to Assisi. On 27 October 1986 some one hundred and sixty of them — Christians of many communions, Jews, Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, and others — kept a day of fasting and pilgrimage in the city of St. Francis.

The pope was careful of the boundaries: the faiths did not pray together as one, but came together to pray, each in its own tongue and place, before gathering in the square of the Lower Basilica. Peace, he told them, is not the product of negotiations and compromises alone; it is the result of prayer. For that one day, it was said, the guns fell silent.

The day gave its name to the "spirit of Assisi," carried on by the Community of Sant'Egidio in yearly meetings of prayer for peace. John Paul II returned to Assisi in January 2002, after the towers fell, and Benedict XVI kept the twenty-fifth anniversary there in 2011.

sources.text: John Paul II, Address to the representatives of the Churches and world religions, Assisi, 27 October 1986 (vatican.va)

title: The execution of Conradin
shortBlurb: The last of the Hohenstaufen, a boy of sixteen, died on the scaffold at Naples, and the long struggle of the Empire and the papacy entered its last act…
body: Conradin was sixteen, grandson of the Emperor Frederick II, and the last hope of his house. Charles of Anjou, called into Italy by the pope and crowned king of Sicily in St. Peter's on 6 January 1266, had slain King Manfred at Benevento; the boy crossed the Alps to claim his inheritance and was received with wild joy, even in Rome.

On 23 August 1268 Charles destroyed his army at Tagliacozzo. Conradin fled, was betrayed into Angevin hands, and on 29 October 1268 was beheaded with his young companion Frederick of Baden on the market-place of Naples. Pope Clement IV had foretold that the gallant youth was being led "like a lamb to the slaughter"; the later tale that the pope counselled his death, the old Catholic historians themselves reject as a fable.

With Conradin the male line of the Hohenstaufen ended, and the Angevin star stood high — but the vengeance of Sicily was preparing. Clement died a month later, on 29 November, and the cardinals then gave the Church the longest vacancy of her history, nearly three years without a pope.

title: The Battle of Río Salado
shortBlurb: Beside Tarifa the kings of Castile and Portugal broke the last great African invasion of Spain, in a battle the pope had blessed as a crusade…
body: Abu al-Hasan, the Marinid sultan of Morocco, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar with the largest African army Spain had seen in a century, and, joined by Yusuf I of Granada, laid siege to Tarifa, the gateway of the Peninsula. Benedict XII blessed the campaign against them as a crusade, and Alfonso XI of Castile and Afonso IV of Portugal made common cause.

On 30 October 1340 the allies gave battle on the banks of the little river Salado, outside Tarifa. A relic of the True Cross, the chronicles tell, was borne before the Christian host; the fighting lasted from mid-morning to noon, when the Portuguese charge broke the Granadan wing and the whole African army dissolved in flight toward the sea.

It was the last time a great army from Africa disputed the soil of Spain: from that day, the old history says, the Spanish Moslems were confined to the kingdom of Granada, which endured until 1492. Alfonso took the name "the Avenger," and the victory is numbered with Las Navas de Tolosa among the decisive days of the Reconquest.
